Load a data file into R

Source: R/io.R
jload.Rd

jload() reads a data file and assigns it as a data frame in your environment. Supports SPSS (.sav), Stata (.dta), SAS (.sas7bdat, .xpt), Excel (.xlsx, .xls), CSV (.csv), and R's native .rds format.

The file format is determined entirely by the file extension — jload() reads the extension (e.g. .sav, .dta, .xlsx) and uses the appropriate reader automatically.

By default, jload() looks for the file in the working directory. If a data folder is configured with joptions(data.dir = ...), that folder is searched first. If a full file path is provided, it is used directly.

The data frame is automatically named after the file (without the extension). Use the name argument to specify a different name.

Usage

jload(
  file,
  name = NULL,
  use = FALSE,
  overwrite = FALSE,
  package = FALSE,
  check.missing = TRUE,
  sheet = NULL,
  skip = 0,
  header = TRUE,
  text = NULL,
  na = NULL,
  preserve.declarations = TRUE,
  missing.notice = NULL,
  quiet = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

file

Character string. The filename (e.g. "mydata.sav") or a full file path (e.g. "C:/Projects/mydata.sav"). Use forward slashes in file paths. If the extension is omitted, jload() searches for common data file types automatically.

name

Character string (optional). The name to assign the data frame in your environment. If omitted, the name is derived from the filename.

use

Logical. If TRUE, automatically calls juse() on the loaded data frame to set it as the default for jstats functions. Default is FALSE.

overwrite

Logical. If TRUE, overwrites an existing object with the same name without prompting. If FALSE (default), prompts for confirmation in interactive sessions. In non-interactive sessions, overwrites and says so in a note. In a script, state it explicitly: jload("mydata.rds", overwrite = TRUE). Otherwise, if the name already exists in your environment, and the script was run by pasting or with RStudio's Run button, the call stops with an error.

package

Logical. If TRUE, loads a jstats example dataset shipped in the package (e.g. community, clinic) by bare name, or a shipped example file by its file name ("community_spss.sav"), bypassing the disk search. Use this when a same-named file in the working directory or data folder would otherwise shadow the shipped copy. If FALSE (default), a matching disk file takes precedence and the shipped copy is used only when no file matches. file must be a name with no path when package = TRUE, and a dataset's name has no extension.

check.missing

Logical. If TRUE (default), scans numeric variables for values that look like coded missing values (e.g. -99, 999) and reports them. Set to FALSE to skip this check.

sheet

For Excel files only. The sheet to read — either a sheet name (character) or sheet number (integer). Defaults to the first sheet. If the file has multiple sheets and sheet is not specified, a message lists the available sheets.

skip

For Excel and CSV files. The number of rows of the sheet, or lines of the file, above the variable names: a title, a blank row, a note. Default 0. When the first row of a sheet looks like a title, a note shows the call with the skip it needs; a CSV file in that shape stops with the same call.

header

For Excel and CSV files. TRUE (default) reads the first row of the sheet, or line of the file, as the variable names. FALSE reads it as the first case, for a file with no names row, and names the variables V1, V2, and so on, as base R's read.csv(header = FALSE) does. Every other format carries its own variable names, so header = FALSE stops there. When every name read is a number, a note shows the call with header = FALSE; writing header = TRUE in the call says the numbers are the names (years, say), and the note is not shown.

text

For Excel and CSV files. Variables to read exactly as the file has them, as text: no number, no TRUE or FALSE, the word NA kept, and na not applied. Name them without quotes, or in quotes, alone or in c(): text = Diag, text = c(Diag, Postcode). A name is the file's own or the one jload() gives the variable ("Post code" or Post_code). For codes that numbers would change, such as the diagnosis codes 250.10 and 250.1. A name a CSV file does not have stops the load before it is read, listing the file's names (a sheet's, once it is read). Every other format carries its own variable types, so text stops there.

na

For Excel and CSV files. Cell values to read as missing, in quotes: na = c("N/A", "-", "."). They are added to what is already missing (an empty cell in a variable of numbers, and in a CSV file the word NA there), in every variable but those named in text. When a variable is numbers except for a few cells, a note names those cells and shows the call with na. Every other format carries its own missing values, so na stops there.

preserve.declarations

Logical. If TRUE (default), declared missing values arriving with the file are preserved: SPSS-style codes such as -99, and declared ranges, keep their original numeric values in the data frame, with the declaration attached so the package's analysis functions still treat them as missing, and Stata-style tagged values (.a, .b, ...) are kept as read. If FALSE, both forms are converted to plain NA on import and the declarations are removed; value labels are kept. Applies to any loaded file whose columns carry missing-value declarations — typically .sav, .dta, and .sas7bdat files, and .rds files saved from such data. For .sav files, TRUE corresponds to haven's user_na = TRUE. The haven package and its documentation call these user-defined missing values.

missing.notice

Per-call override for the missing-value notification. NULL (default) defers to the setting from joutput(). TRUE prints the notification, in its full form, on any load with declared missing values; FALSE suppresses it. Under the default (standard) and full output levels the first such load in a session prints the full notification and later loads print a compact form (the variable inventory, plus the convention note when one applies, without the guidance lines); minimal suppresses the notification. See ?joutput for the full toggle behavior.

quiet

Logical; default FALSE. When TRUE, suppresses jload()'s informational messages (the directory-resolution note, file found, load summary, default-data note, registration notes, and the narrative about declared missing values, overriding missing.notice). Errors, warnings, the multi-sheet advisory, the overwrite prompt, the note that a local file shadowed a shipped dataset, the note that an existing object was replaced, and the notes on what the read changed or found (variable names changed, a title row, names that are all numbers, rows and columns that may not be data, a CSV file's encoding, a variable kept as text, a variable of numbers made text by a few cells) are still shown, as is the coded-missing scan report; turn that off with check.missing = FALSE.

...

Not used. An input jload() does not take – a misspelled argument – stops with "unused input" and the name as typed, in place of R's own "unused argument".

Value

Invisibly returns NULL; jload() is called for its side effects. The loaded data frame is placed in the calling environment under the file's name (or name), and any classification registrations saved with an .rds file are restored for that name. Loading a file that carries none clears any registrations set this session under that name, with a note saying so. Do not assign the result: x <- jload("mydata.rds") binds only NULL, while the data frame still arrives under its own name.

Details

File paths: Use forward slashes (/) in file paths. If you copy a path from Windows File Explorer, replace the backslashes with forward slashes. R does not accept single backslashes in file paths: inside quoted text it reads a backslash and the letter after it as one special character (a backslash before t is a tab), so the path that arrives is not the one typed. jload() stops on such a path and shows it written with forward slashes.

CSV files: A CSV file with one column keeps its empty lines: each is a case whose one cell is empty, which is how a missing value is written there. In a file with two or more columns an empty line is not a case. An empty cell in a text variable is read as blank text, never as missing (see jsave).

Before a CSV file is read, every line's values are counted. A first line with fewer values than the lines below it (a title above the names, or a name missing), and a later line with more values than the first, stop the load with the line and what to do: read as they are, R would turn the first values of every line into row names, or split the long line into two cases, and say nothing. A file whose values are separated by semicolons, as Excel saves them in many European settings, stops with the base R line that reads it. A file that is not in UTF-8 (one saved by Excel on Windows as "CSV (Comma delimited)" is in Windows-1252) is read in Windows-1252, and a note says so. Read with header = FALSE, a file has no names line, so each line is measured against the number of values most lines hold: a line holding more stops the load, and one holding fewer is read with its last cells empty.

Values in a CSV file: A CSV file stores every value as text, so each variable's type is read from its values. A variable becomes numbers, or TRUE and FALSE, only where no value would change:

  • A whole number written with a leading zero (a postcode 0800, an ID 007) keeps its variable as text, as written; numbers would drop the zero. A note says so, with the line that makes it numbers anyway (and, for a variable jload() renamed, the line that puts its label back).

  • A whole number of more than 15 digits (an account or record ID) keeps its variable as text: a number holds 15 digits exactly, so different IDs would become one number. A note says so.

  • T and F standing alone stay text (a variable of F in a sample of women is not FALSE); the words TRUE and FALSE, as R and Excel write them, are read as TRUE and FALSE.

  • The word NA is missing in a variable of numbers, or of TRUE and FALSE, which is how R writes a missing value there. In a text variable it is a word, as in an Excel sheet (NA is Namibia's country code), and the coded-missing scan names it with the line that declares it missing.

Base R's read.csv() reads all four as numbers, TRUE or FALSE, or missing, without a word. Use text for a code the rules cannot see, such as 250.10, which numbers would read as 250.1.

Values that are not numbers: In a CSV file or a sheet, a variable of numbers that holds a few other values – N/A, - or . for a missing value – is read as text. jstats does not assume such a value is missing (a dash can mean zero), so a note names the values, with the jload() call whose na reads them as missing: jload("incomes.csv", overwrite = TRUE, na = c("N/A", "-")). A variable is named when it has at most five such values and numbers in more than half of its cells that are not empty; in a sheet, number cells must be more than half of them. A sheet's variable that also holds a number stored as text stays text whatever na names, so its note gives the base R lines that make it numbers instead: d$Code[d$Code == "N/A"] <- NA, then d$Code <- as.numeric(d$Code). Where jload() renamed the variable, a last line puts back the label it gave it, which as.numeric() drops.

A file with no names row: A CSV file or a sheet whose first row is data loses that case to the variable names, which are then numbers (1 becomes X1). When every name read is a number, or empty, a note says the row they came from may be the first case and shows the call that reads it as one: jload("scores.csv", header = FALSE), the variables named V1, V2, and so on.

Rows and columns that may not be data: A sheet can hold rows with nothing in them, a column with no name and nothing in it, and lines of text below the data, such as a source or a footnote; a CSV file can hold a line of commas alone, an empty column from a comma at the end of each line, and the row numbers R's write.csv() writes in a first column with no name. Each is read as data, as a case or a variable, and a note names them by their place in the file, with the case numbers or the variable names; when footnotes turned a variable of numbers into text, it says so. Nothing is removed. An empty line in a CSV file of one column is a case with a missing value, and is not named.

Variable names from other software: A file from outside R can hold names R cannot use as they are: 2024 score, Age (years), an empty header, two columns with the same name, a word R reserves (if, TRUE), an SPSS name such as Q1@A, a Stata name such as _merge. For every format but .rds, each such name is changed: spaces and symbols at either end are dropped, any other run of characters that are not letters, digits or underscores becomes one underscore, a name that starts with a digit or an underscore or is a reserved word gets an X in front, an empty name becomes V and its column's position, a repeated name gets _2, and a changed name is kept to 32 characters. So 2024 score becomes X2024_score and Age (years) becomes Age_years. A name R can use as it is is never changed. The original name becomes the variable's label, unless the variable has a label of its own, and a note lists every change. An .rds file is returned as it was saved.

File search order:

  1. If the path contains a directory separator (/, or a backslash), the path is used directly.

  2. If the path is a bare filename, jload() checks: (a) the folder named by the data.dir setting in joptions if it is set and exists; (b) the working directory.

When the extension is omitted, both locations are searched for every supported extension, and more than one match (two extensions, or the same file in both locations) is an error that asks for the extension. If nothing matches on disk, a bare name falls back to a shipped example dataset of that name (see below).

Auto-naming: The data frame name is derived from the filename by stripping the extension. If the resulting name starts with a digit (which R does not allow as a variable name), you must supply the name argument; the error offers one (2024.csv is offered name = "X2024"). Other characters R does not allow in a name, such as spaces and hyphens, are changed as variable names are (see above): "my data-1.sav" loads as my_data_1.

Excel files: Excel files (.xlsx, .xls) do not contain variable or value labels. The data will be loaded as plain numeric, character, or logical columns; a variable whose name was changed has its original name as its label. Use jrelabel() to add labels after loading if needed. Row 1 of the sheet is read as the variable names; when the names are lower down, skip gives the number of rows above them, and when there are none, header = FALSE reads row 1 as data. Each variable's type is read from every row of the sheet.

Missing-value declarations: Missing-value declarations are stored in the file itself, but they only survive the trip back if the reader requests them. jload() always does, so declarations written by jsave() are present after every jstats load (unless preserve.declarations = FALSE). Other ways of reading the same file may convert the declared cells to plain NA and discard the declarations, so the same file can show different numbers of valid cases depending on how it was read.

Coded missing values: When check.missing = TRUE, the function scans numeric variables for values that look like coded missing values but are not declared as missing. (Declared missing values are reported in the load's own notification, never by the scan.) Only whole-number values are considered. A value is flagged when it is

  • a negative number at least three times the size of the variable's largest non-negative value (-99 on a 1-to-5 scale), or

  • at least five times the size of every other value in the variable (999 on a 1-to-7 scale).

A value in the missing.convention.codes setting of joptions (-99, -98 and -97 by default) is flagged as well, whatever its size. A flagged value whose value label suggests missingness (such as "Refused" or "Don't know") is reported as label-only; one of the setting's codes, as convention-matched; the rest as suspected. Flagged values are reported but not changed. If they are missing values, declare them with jdeclare_missing, which keeps the codes and their labels; the report shows the call.

A text variable's values are flagged too: as label-only when their value label suggests missingness, and as suspected when the value itself does ("UNKNOWN", "Not stated") or when it differs from a value the variable declares only in letter case or outer spaces. The call the report shows names the values the variable already declares, since a declaration replaces them, and at most three in all.

Package example datasets and .rda / .RData files: jload() opens the example datasets shipped with jstats – currently community and clinic – by bare name: jload("community"). These ship inside the package as .rda files, but the bare-name load is a lookup of the shipped dataset, not a file read, and it works only for package datasets. It does not extend to .rda or .RData files generally: naming the extension (jload("community.rda")) or pointing at any other .rda or .RData file is refused with a pointer to base R's load(), because such files can hold several objects under names of their own choosing, outside jload's one-data-frame contract. Note also that the shipped dataset is a fallback: a file with a matching name in the working directory or data.dir folder is opened instead of the shipped copy. Use package = TRUE to force the shipped dataset.

Example files: jstats also ships the community data as files, the kind a collaborator might send: community_spss.sav, community_stata.dta and community_excel.xlsx. When no file of that name is in the data.dir folder or the working directory, jload("community_spss.sav") reads the shipped one, and says so; the name without its extension works too (jload("community_spss")). A file of the same name on disk is read instead, with a note giving the call that reads the shipped file: jload("community_spss.sav", package = TRUE).

Variables named T or F: At joutput("full") a note names a variable called T or F. jstats reads it as the variable, but in base R T and F also stand for TRUE and FALSE, and code run inside the data frame – with(), subset() – reads the variable in their place.

See also

jstats for the package overview, workflow conventions, and complete function listing.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
# SPSS
jload("community.sav")
jload("community.sav", use = TRUE)
jload("community.sav", name = "MySurvey")

# Stata
jload("community.dta")

# SAS
jload("community.sas7bdat")
jload("community.xpt")

# Excel
jload("community.xlsx")
jload("community.xlsx", sheet = "Wave2")
jload("community.xlsx", sheet = 2)
jload("survey.xlsx", skip = 2)   # a title and a blank row above the names
jload("scores.csv", header = FALSE)   # no names row: V1, V2, ...
jload("visits.csv", text = Diag)       # codes kept as written: 250.10
jload("incomes.csv", na = c("N/A", "-"))   # these cells read as missing

# CSV and R format
jload("community.csv")
jload("community.rds")

# Extension omitted -- jload searches for a matching file automatically
jload("community")

# The example files shipped with jstats, read by name
jload("community_spss.sav")
jload("community_excel.xlsx", package = TRUE)   # even beside a local copy

# Full file path
jload("C:/Projects/Data/community.dta")

# Quiet load (e.g. in a .Rprofile or startup script): suppresses the
# informational messages while still loading. Errors and warnings still show.
jload("community.rds", name = "MyData", quiet = TRUE)
} # }
